questions.q: How does this lesson resolve the categorization conflict between St. Catherine's, Lakeshore, and Prairie View?
options: A shared corporate-level top category list, with domain-specific subcategories each hospital system configures for itself
By adopting St. Catherine's full multi-tier scheme as the mandatory standard for all three systems
By giving each hospital system a completely separate ServiceNow instance
By leaving ticket categorization as free text indefinitely for all three systems
questions.explain: The two-layer model lets St. Catherine's keep its reporting detail, Lakeshore keep local governance, and Prairie View gain real structure, without fully satisfying any one system's original ask.

questions.q: What does Phase 1 of this workstream actually include, as scoped in this lesson?
options: Incident and request management on one shared catalog front door, with domain-scoped queues and basic domain/corporate reporting
HR service delivery and facilities management for all three hospital systems
A fully built virtual agent and chatbot front end
Advanced analytics dashboards built before the Service Desk goes live
questions.explain: Phase 1 is the core unified Service Desk capability — the workstream Lesson 12 scoped this chapter around.

questions.q: Why are HR service delivery and facilities management explicitly deferred out of Phase 1?
options: They were already scoped as later phases of the same eighteen-month rollout, and bundling them in now would reintroduce the all-at-once risk this chapter is avoiding
Because Technical Architecture decided Meridian should never implement them
Because they require a completely different ServiceNow instance
Because no stakeholder at any of the three hospital systems asked for them
questions.explain: Deferring them is a deliberate, stated project decision tied to the same reasoning that scoped this chapter to one workstream in the first place, not a sign they're unimportant.

questions.q: What does this lesson's timeline do differently from a single simultaneous cutover across all three hospital systems?
options: It stages go-live, starting with a pilot at one system and rolling out to the others afterward, keeping legacy processes live until each system's own cutover
It launches all three systems on the same day with no pilot
It removes each system's legacy help-desk process immediately at project kickoff
It skips training entirely to meet the eighteen-month deadline
questions.explain: A staged go-live, with legacy processes supported until each system's own replacement is working, is the plan's concrete answer to Prairie View's trust concern.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does deferring advanced reporting and analytics dashboards make sense?
options: Because they depend on a live Service Desk generating real data, so building them first would mean designing against guesses
Because no hospital system at Meridian will ever need reporting
Because basic domain and corporate reporting is impossible to build in Phase 1
Because the board explicitly banned any future reporting work
questions.explain: Reporting and analytics are deferred with a stated technical reason — they need real operational data to be designed well, not an arbitrary cut.
